# Using ISLA {#sec-using}

**ISLA ships as one class with one reference configuration, trained and
evaluated by the unified external-aerodynamics recipe. This chapter is the
operating manual.** It tells you which configuration to run and what the
few remaining options are for. It states what the model needs from your
data and the commands that train and evaluate it. It tells you how to set
the learning rate when you change the width or depth, how to use the
inference sampler that removes most of the draw noise at a fixed cell
budget, how to load a checkpoint, and what a step costs. Everything here is
about ISLA unless an option is named. The reasons behind each
recommendation are in @sec-isla and the evidence chapters, cited where they
apply.

```{python}
#| label: setup-using
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
```

## Which configuration {#sec-using-config}

**Run ISLA as the class ships it: cosine routing, the RMS-pairwise-distance
length unit, the fused geometry kernel where it can run, and interior
queries carrying a share of the total boundary measure.** Those are the
class defaults, so `ISLA(outputs=..., global_inputs=...)` with nothing else
is the reference configuration. The recipe's `isla_surface.yaml` names the
fields, fixes the dimensions and states the frame setting explicitly:

```yaml
model:
  _target_: physicsnemo.experimental.models.ISLA
  outputs:              # the dataset's targets, by name and tensor rank
    pressure: 0         #   rank 0: a scalar field
    wss: 1              #   rank 1: a vector field (a stress tensor would be {rank: 2, symmetric: true})
  global_inputs:
    freestream: 1       # one rank-1 global input: the far-field flow direction
  hidden: 384                 # the reference configuration; also the class defaults
  n_layers: 12
  n_slices: 256
  mlp_ratio: 4
  scale_mode: rms_distance    # length unit = measure-weighted RMS pairwise distance of the sample (the frame has no origin)
  geo_kernel: null            # automatic: the fused Triton kernel on CUDA with one to three global vectors, the eager region otherwise
```

The reference configuration is 384 wide with 12 layers and 256 slices, at
learning rate 5e-4 (the reference selection, @sec-nb-ref-verdict). The
class defaults and the recipe's `isla_surface` and `isla_volume` state the
same dimensions. This is the one place the book states them, and the width
and depth ladders of @sec-review-frontier are deviations from it. Lanes of
the earlier protocol ran 192 wide at 1e-3 and are labeled so wherever they
appear. ISLA has one frame and one routing form. The rows below are the
options that remain on it.

| configuration | recipe config | when to use | what you give up |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ISLA** (cosine routing, RMS-pairwise-distance length unit, fused geometry kernel, `query_mass: source_total`) | `isla_surface`, `isla_volume` | every new surface or interior task | nothing among ISLA's options; the standing against GeoTransolver and Transolver, dataset by dataset and task by task, is in @sec-surface and @sec-interior |
| query mass `geometric_mean` (`query_mass: geometric_mean`) | option on `isla_volume`, `isla_volume_support` | interior tasks only, when a boundary is guaranteed to arrive at one fixed refinement | the refinement contract: each query's routing weight becomes the mean boundary log-weight plus a learned offset, so re-representing the same surface on finer cells shifts the balance between surface and queries (@sec-isla-contracts) |

Every checkpoint stores its constructor arguments, so a model saved under
any option loads in the configuration that trained it (@sec-using-checkpoint).

::: {.callout-note title="When query independence is required"}
Both configurations above predict at a point as a function of the whole
request. Deploy an interior surrogate built from `isla_volume` at its
training query count (@sec-using-checkpoint). If a deployment needs the
prediction at a point to be exactly the same whatever else is asked for
(chunked or streaming inference over arbitrary point sets, or a per-point
answer that must not change between requests), use the read-only decoder
behind `query_independent: true`. It can take a per-case interacting
support set (`support_tokens: true`; recipe config `isla_volume_support`).
It holds the contract exactly and is several times less accurate than the
interacting decode on every interior field. What it is, what it costs and
when it is worth the price are in @sec-arch-passive-decoder.
:::

## What the model needs from your data {#sec-using-inputs}

**ISLA takes three geometry arrays per case plus named fields of declared
rank. The two that are easy to get wrong are the measure weights, which
must sum to the boundary's measure, and the global directions, which must
be directions.** The forward call is keyword-only, so the recipe's
`forward_kwargs:` mapping reads exactly as the call does. The field names
under `global_inputs`, `boundary_inputs` and `query_inputs` are the ones
the model block declares, with their ranks. The model returns a TensorDict
keyed by the `outputs:` names (`output_type: fields`). For the surface
task:

```yaml
forward_kwargs:
  points: interior.points                                  # (B, N, 3) sampled cell centroids ("interior" is the datapipe's name for the sampled point set, not the fluid domain)
  normals: boundaries.vehicle.cell_data.normals            # (B, N, 3) unit outward normals
  measure_weights: interior.point_data._effective_measure   # (B, N) area each sampled cell stands for
  global_inputs:
    freestream: global_data.U_inf_dir                      # (B, 3) the one global direction of external aerodynamics
```

Three of these need a word.

- **The measure weights must sum to the boundary's measure.** When the
  recipe keeps $n$ of $N$ cells, each kept cell carries the Horvitz–Thompson
  weight: its area times $N/n$. The weights then stand for the full surface
  at any `sampling_resolution`, and the routing's quadrature sums read the
  surface area rather than the retained fraction of it. The length unit
  normalizes the weights and is indifferent to the factor, but the
  quadrature sums are not. The surface dataset stores this in
  `interior.point_data._effective_measure`. The volume dataset uses
  `boundaries.vehicle.cell_data._effective_measure` through its
  `ComposeQuadratureMeasure` stage. Both are complete measures, including
  sampling corrections. Point measures carry their represented dimension
  and follow geometric scaling: on a two-dimensional problem such as
  AirfRANS the measure is the segment length.
- **A rank-1 global input is a direction.** The problem's global
  directions (the rank-1 entries of `global_inputs`) enter as unit vectors.
  The model normalizes each again internally and discards its magnitude.
  For external aerodynamics `ComputeFreestreamDirection` writes `U_inf_dir`
  from the solver's velocity. This is also the fair-comparison rule for
  every architecture in the book (@sec-unit-direction-rule).
- **A magnitude that matters is a rank-0 global input.** Declare it
  (`u_inf: 0`; a standardized parameter vector is `params: {rank: 0,
  channels: 6}`) and pass it under its name. No fixed power of a far-field
  speed is a physical law for every output (a pressure coefficient is degree
  zero, a dimensional pressure degree two), so the model learns the
  dependence like any other parameter. The AirfRANS configuration passes
  the inlet speed this way (`global_data.U_inf_mag`).

For the interior task the model needs one more array, the query positions,
and nothing else about them. `isla_volume` adds

```yaml
forward_kwargs:
  points: boundaries.vehicle.cell_centroids
  normals: boundaries.vehicle.cell_normals
  measure_weights: boundaries.vehicle.cell_data._effective_measure
  global_inputs:
    freestream: global_data.U_inf_dir
  query_points: interior.points          # (B, Q, 3); direction and wall distance are derived inside the model
```

The model computes each query's direction and signed distance to the wall
from the boundary sample (the nearest boundary cell, @sec-arch-modes). No
signed-distance field has to be stored, sampled or declared. The distance
is to the sampled boundary, not the full mesh. The `isla_volume_provided`
configuration keeps the dataset's full-mesh field instead
(`interior_geometry: provided`, with `query_normals:
interior.point_data.sdf_normals` and `query_inputs: {sdf:
interior.point_data.sdf}`). It exists to measure that difference
(@sec-nb-internal-geometry-prereg) and to load interior checkpoints trained
with it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Nested field names"}
A dataset that stores its fields in groups (`solution/pressure` on disk,
`solution.pressure` in a config) names its targets with a dot, and the
model's `outputs:` block uses the same dotted names. A dot is the only way
to spell a group, because every value of `outputs`, `global_inputs`,
`boundary_inputs` and `query_inputs` is a rank spec. So
`outputs: {"solution.pressure": 0, "solution.velocity": 1}` declares two
leaves of one group. The model returns a TensorDict in which
`out["solution", "pressure"]` and `out["solution"]["pressure"]` both
address the first. The recipe reads its targets by the same dotted names,
so `output_type: fields` consumes the nested output unchanged. The input
mappings accept a flat dict with dotted names, a nested dict, or a
TensorDict.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Problems other than external aerodynamics"}
The architecture knows only that it was handed named fields of declared
rank. A buoyant flow passes gravity as its one direction. A magnetized flow
passes two. Steady conduction with pinned temperatures passes no direction
and supplies the pinned values as a rank-0 boundary input
(`boundary_inputs: {trace: 0}`). An elasticity problem passes its
prescribed displacement and traction as rank-1 boundary inputs
(`bc_displacement: 1`, `bc_traction: 1`). A planar dataset that stored the
components separately stacks them with `StackScalarFields` in its dataset
yaml. It predicts the stress as a symmetric rank-2 output
(`stress: {rank: 2, symmetric: true}`), and the recipe reads off its
laboratory components for a `symmetric_tensor` target. Each global
direction adds one seed cosine, one relational cosine and two vectors to
the output basis. Each rank-1 boundary input adds its frame cosines and
norm to the seed and one relational cosine per slice
(@sec-isla-inputs-rank). The tests in `test_isla_global_inputs.py`,
`test_isla_inputs.py` and `test_isla_heads.py` cover zero and two
directions, global scalars, rank-1 and rank-2 inputs and every output rank
and parity. The frame-input and rank-1-input solids configurations run the
fused geometry kernel; its limits are in @sec-isla-inputs-rank and the
switch in @sec-using-cost.
:::

## Training {#sec-using-train}

**Train at the recipe defaults, 200,000 sampled cells per case for 500
epochs at learning rate 5e-4, with no augmentation. The only setting that
needs thought is the learning rate when you leave width 384.** From the
recipe root:

```bash
# DrivAerML Surface task (sampling_resolution defaults to 200,000 cells per case).
# compile=false is the configuration of the evidence lanes; the compiled path computes the same function faster.
# The ISLA configs pin training.optimizer.lr=5e-4; it is stated here so the protocol is explicit.
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=5e-4 compile=false

# DrivAerML Volume task: boundary -> interior, queries as interacting tokens; the queries' direction and
# wall distance are computed inside the model from the boundary sample (model=isla_volume_provided reads
# the dataset's full-mesh signed-distance field instead).
python src/train.py model=isla_volume dataset=drivaer_ml_volume_reference \
    training.optimizer.lr=5e-4 compile=false

# HiLiftAeroML surface (the 200,000-cell default again; 500 epochs, as on the cars)
python src/train.py model=isla_surface dataset=highlift_surface \
    training.optimizer.lr=5e-4 compile=false training.num_epochs=500
```

These commands are the reporting protocol of @sec-protocol. ISLA needs no
rotation augmentation. The contracts make it exact, and a model trained in
the dataset's native frame predicts a body in any pose (@sec-pose).

### The learning rate {#sec-using-lr}

**Use 5e-4 at the reference width 384 and 12 layers. For a wider or deeper
model, start from $10^{-3} \times 192 / \mathrm{hidden} \times 12 /
\mathrm{layers}$ and treat it as a starting rate, not a limit.** The
expression gives $10^{-3}$ at width 192, $5 \times 10^{-4}$ at 384,
$2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ at 768, and $2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ at 384 wide and 24
layers. Every width and depth in the capacity ladders trains cleanly at
this rate, and the ladders of @sec-review-frontier run at it. A model
trained at the rule rate is therefore comparable with the book's lanes.
Under ISLA's cosine routing the logits are bounded, so the routing-collapse
failure that would otherwise set a hard ceiling on the rate is unreachable
(@sec-isla-routing-forms). A higher rate is an experiment, not a hazard.
The recipe's ISLA configurations pin 5e-4 rather than inheriting the
recipe-wide default. The interior standings of @sec-interior are the
reference configuration's at 5e-4. GeoTransolver-volume trains at 1e-3,
its best rate there.

## Evaluation and the inference sampler {#sec-using-sampler}

**Score in float32 at the reporting protocol's 200,000 cells. If the cell
budget is fixed and smaller, draw the cells with the stratified sampler.**
Inference shares the training configuration and reads the checkpoint by run
identifier:

```bash
# sampling_resolution=200000 is the reporting protocol; the infer default is the whole mesh
python src/infer.py model=isla_surface dataset=drivaer_ml_surface \
    run_id=<the trained run_id> infer_split=val sampling_resolution=200000 precision=float32
```

Report in float32. The recipe trains under bf16 autocast, and every number
in this book is a float32 inference on the final-epoch checkpoint
(@sec-metrics). A bf16 inference differs from the float32 one by rounding
of order a percent. Under a rigid motion of the input, its prediction moves
by several percent, where the float32 prediction moves at the level of
float32 roundoff (the residuals are tabulated in @sec-isla-contracts). If
the pose or the sampling-consistency contract is load-bearing, infer in
float32.

**For inference at a fixed cell budget, draw the cells with the stratified
sampler.** Replace the dataset's `SubsampleMesh` stage with the recipe's
`StratifiedSubsampleMesh`:

```yaml
    - _target_: ${dp:StratifiedSubsampleMesh}   # in place of SubsampleMesh
      n_cells: ${sampling_resolution}
```

It keeps the same inclusion law (every cell kept with probability $n/N$,
weight $N/n$), so nothing about the trained model or the quantity it
estimates changes. The kept cells are a *systematic* draw along the Morton
order of the cell centroids: one cell per consecutive run of $N/n$ cells,
with a single random offset. The Morton order sorts cells by interleaved
coordinate bits, a space-filling curve along which consecutive cells are
spatial neighbors. A systematic sample has the same expectation as an
independent draw for every cell-weighted integral and a lower variance for
smooth integrands. The effect is a free improvement for every model and
largest for ISLA, whose slice states are the noisiest estimates
(@sec-deficit-anatomy).

The book keeps the independent draw for its headline comparisons. For a
deployment, use the stratified draw or more cells.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="How many cells"}
Use 200,000 cells. Error is flat above 100,000 (@sec-equal-budget). If the
budget forces fewer cells, use the stratified draw.
:::

## Loading a trained model {#sec-using-checkpoint}

**A checkpoint carries its own constructor arguments, so loading is one
call and the forward call mirrors the recipe mapping.** A saved ISLA is a
PhysicsNeMo module checkpoint and loads with the class's `from_checkpoint`.
No configuration has to be repeated:

```python
from physicsnemo.experimental.models import ISLA
model = ISLA.from_checkpoint("checkpoints/isla_surface.mdlus").eval()
out = model(points=x, normals=n, measure_weights=w, global_inputs={"freestream": g_hat})
p, tau = out["pressure"], out["wss"]  # (B, N) and (B, N, 3)
```

`points` and `normals` are (B, N, 3). `measure_weights` is (B, N) and sums
to the boundary's measure. `global_inputs` is a mapping from each declared
name to its tensor: (B, 3) for a direction, (B,) or (B, channels) for a
rank-0 field. The output is a TensorDict of batch size (B, N) keyed by the
declared output names (a dotted name is a nested leaf), each field with as
many trailing axes of size 3 as its rank. For interior prediction with
`isla_volume`, add `query_points` (B, Q, 3) and read the output at the
query rows. The model derives each query's direction and signed wall
distance from the boundary sample. A checkpoint trained with
`interior_geometry: provided` takes `query_normals` and
`query_inputs={"sdf": ...}` instead, as its constructor arguments record.
Deploy at the training query count (200,000 at the reporting protocol on
DrivAerML), because the interacting decode's prediction at a point depends
on the joint query set (@sec-interior-companion).

## Cost {#sec-using-cost}


```{python}
#| label: para-using-cost-lede
#| output: asis
CSW = {r["arm"]: r for r in json.load(open(RES / "cost_sweep_ref_gb300_bf16_2026-09-22.json"))["runs"] if r["tokens"] == 200000 and r["status"] == "ok"}
_med = lambda v: sorted(v)[len(v) // 2]
_isla, _gt, _gt512 = CSW["isla_ref_r1_384x12_cos_fused"], CSW["geotransolver_256"], CSW["geotransolver_512"]
print(f"**At the reporting protocol of 200,000 cells per case, ISLA trains at {_isla['peak_allocated_gib'] / _gt['peak_allocated_gib']:.2f}x "
      f"GeoTransolver-256's peak memory and {_med(_isla['step_ms']) / _med(_gt['step_ms']):.2f}x its step time. GeoTransolver-512, "
      f"the parameter match, costs {_med(_gt512['step_ms']) / _med(_isla['step_ms']):.2f}x ISLA's step time and "
      f"{_gt512['peak_allocated_gib'] / _isla['peak_allocated_gib']:.1f}x its memory.** @tbl-isla-cost reads the three footprints from one "
      "cost sweep on one GB300.")
```
 The step is memory-bound at every stage
but the MLP. The per-slice geometry (separations, invariants, routing
softmaxes) is most of the stored activations. That is why the eager path
rebuilds it in the backward pass instead of storing it (`geo_checkpoint`,
bitwise identical outputs and gradients), and why a fused Triton kernel
exists for the geometry region. `geo_kernel: null` resolves to the kernel
at the first forward pass wherever it can run, and to the eager recompute
region elsewhere (@sec-arch-switches; the conditions are in the list
below). Every path computes the same function (output relative L2 against
the eager reference at most $5.5 \times 10^{-7}$ in bf16,
@sec-nb-geokernel-auto). That footprint is what buys accuracy at scale. On
the DrivAerML Surface task at 435 cars, ISLA reaches GeoTransolver's floor
at less than a third of the memory (@sec-shared-floor).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-isla-cost
#| output: asis
rows = [("ISLA (reference configuration, fused kernel)", "isla_ref_r1_384x12_cos_fused"), ("GeoTransolver-256", "geotransolver_256"), ("GeoTransolver-512 (the parameter match)", "geotransolver_512")]
out = "| architecture | parameters | peak memory per device [GiB] | median step [ms] | ÷ ISLA: parameters | ÷ ISLA: memory | ÷ ISLA: step |\n|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|\n"
i = CSW[rows[0][1]]
for lab, k in rows:
    c = CSW[k]
    out += (f"| {lab} | {c['n_params']/1e6:.1f}M | {c['peak_allocated_gib']:.1f} | {_med(c['step_ms']):.0f} | {c['n_params']/i['n_params']:.2f}x | "
            f"{c['peak_allocated_gib']/i['peak_allocated_gib']:.2f}x | {_med(c['step_ms'])/_med(i['step_ms']):.2f}x |\n")
print(out)
print(": Training cost at the reporting protocol on the DrivAerML Surface task: one case of 200,000 sampled cells per step, bfloat16 autocast, "
      "one GB300, forward plus backward, each architecture as the recipe trains it (ISLA on the fused geometry kernel, GeoTransolver compiled). Memory "
      "is the peak allocated by the step; the step is the median over the timed steps. How to read this: the table states cost, not accuracy (the "
      "standing of these configurations is in @sec-surface); the ratio columns are each architecture ÷ ISLA, above one meaning the architecture "
      "costs more. It does not show Transolver, whose row is in @tbl-cost-200k, nor the eager geometry region, which computes the same function "
      "at about three times the memory (@sec-cost-sweep). "
      "Data: results/cost_sweep_ref_gb300_bf16_2026-09-22.json. {#tbl-isla-cost}")
```

Two practical consequences:

- **Leave `geo_kernel` at its default (`null`).** On CUDA with one to three
  global directions, the model selects the fused kernel at the first
  forward pass and logs the choice. Off CUDA, with rank-2 per-token inputs,
  or with more than three vectors in all, it falls back to the eager
  recompute region. Force `eager` only to reproduce the exact arithmetic
  path of a checkpoint trained on the eager region.
- **On the eager path, leave `geo_checkpoint: true` unless you are short
  of time and long on memory.** It is bitwise identical in outputs and
  gradients. Under the fused kernel the recompute is built in and the flag
  has no effect.

## Contracts you can check on your own data {#sec-using-contracts}

**Each contract is a one-line test on a loaded checkpoint, and a residual
far above float32 rounding points at the inputs, not the model.** The
contracts are exact properties of the code (@sec-isla-contracts), and each
is cheap to test on a loaded checkpoint. Rotate and translate the inputs by
a random rigid motion, then compare the scalars (unchanged) and the vectors
(rotated). Scale the points by $k$ and the measure weights by $k^2$
(unchanged). Scale the measure weights alone (unchanged). In float32 the
residuals on the trained checkpoints are at the level of float32 roundoff.
In bf16 autocast they are several percent, mostly rounding
(@sec-isla-contracts). A residual far above these on your own data points
at the inputs, not the model: normals with inconsistent orientation,
weights that do not sum to the boundary's measure, or positions that were
centered or scaled by something sample-dependent before the model saw them.
The model normalizes the normals and the global vectors itself, so their
magnitudes cannot cause a residual.
